text:
CYRANO:
  A kiss! The word is sweet.
  I do not see why your lip does not dare it;
  If it already burns her, what will the thing itself be?
  Do not make it into something terrifying:
  Did you not, just now, almost imperceptibly,
  Leave banter behind and glide without alarm
  From smile to sigh, and from sigh to tears!
  Glide a little farther, imperceptibly:
  From tears to a kiss there is but a shiver!

ROXANE:
  Be quiet!

CYRANO:
  A kiss—when all is said and done, what is it?
  An oath made at somewhat closer quarters, a promise
  More precise, a confession that seeks confirmation,
  A rosy dot placed over the i in the verb to love;
  It is a secret that takes the mouth for an ear,
  An instant of infinity that makes the sound of a bee,
  A communion with the taste of a flower,
  A way of breathing in a little of each other's heart,
  And of tasting a little of each other's soul upon the lips!

ROXANE:
  Be quiet!

CYRANO:
  A kiss is so noble, Madame,
  That the queen of France allowed the happiest of lords
  To take one from her—the queen herself!

ROXANE:
  Well then!

CYRANO (growing impassioned):
  Like Buckingham, I suffered in silence;
  Like him, I adore the queen that you are;
  Like him, I am sorrowful and faithful...

ROXANE:
  And you are
  Handsome like him!

CYRANO (aside, brought back to earth):
  That is true, I am handsome—I had forgotten!

ROXANE:
  Well, then! Climb up and pluck this peerless flower...

CYRANO (pushing Christian toward the balcony):
  Climb!

ROXANE:
  This taste of the heart...

CYRANO:
  Climb!

ROXANE:
  This sound of a bee...

CYRANO:
  Climb!

CHRISTIAN (hesitating):
  But now it seems to me that this is wrong!

ROXANE:
  This instant of infinity!...

CYRANO (pushing him):
  Climb, then, you animal!
  (Christian springs forward and, by way of the bench, the foliage, and the pillars,
  reaches the balusters and climbs over them.)

CHRISTIAN:
  Ah, Roxane!
  (He embraces her and bends over her lips.)

CYRANO:
  Ow! What a strange pang in my heart!
  —Kiss, feast of love at which I am Lazarus!
  Here in the darkness, a crumb of you comes to me—
  Yes, I feel my heart receiving you a little,
  Since upon that lip where Roxane is deceived,
  She kisses the words I spoke just now!
  (The theorbos are heard):
  A sad tune, a merry tune: the Capuchin!
  (He pretends to run as though arriving from far away, and calls in a clear voice):
  Ho there!

ROXANE:
  What is it?

CYRANO:
  Me. I was passing by... Is Christian still here?

CHRISTIAN (greatly surprised):
  Why, Cyrano!

ROXANE:
  Good day, cousin!

CYRANO:
  Good day, cousin!

ROXANE:
  I am coming down!
  (She disappears into the house. At the back, the Capuchin reenters.)

CHRISTIAN (catching sight of him):
  Oh! Again!
  (He follows Roxane.)



Scene 3.XI.

Cyrano, Christian, Roxane, the Capuchin, Ragueneau.


THE CAPUCHIN:
  It is here—I insist—
  Magdeleine Robin!

CYRANO:
  You said: Ro-lin.

THE CAPUCHIN:
  No: Bin. B, i, n, bin!

ROXANE (appearing on the threshold of the house, followed by Ragueneau,
  who is carrying a lantern, and by Christian):
  What is it?

THE CAPUCHIN:
  A letter.

CHRISTIAN:
  What?

THE CAPUCHIN (to Roxane):
  Oh! It can only concern something holy!
  It is a worthy lord who...

ROXANE (to Christian):
  It is De Guiche!

CHRISTIAN:
  He dares?...

ROXANE:
  Oh! But he is not going to pester me forever!
  (Breaking the seal on the letter):
  I love you, and if...
  (By the light of Ragueneau's lantern, she reads in a low voice, apart):
  Mademoiselle,
  The drums
  Are beating; my regiment is fastening its surcoats;
  It is leaving; as for me, they think I have already left: I am staying.
  I disobey you. I am in this convent.
  I am about to come, and I inform you beforehand
  Through a friar as simple as a goat,
  Who can understand nothing of this. Your lip
  Smiled too much at me earlier: I wished to see it again.
  Send everyone away, and deign to receive
  The audacious man who is already forgiven, I hope,
  And who signs himself your most... et cetera...
  (To the Capuchin):
  Father,
  Here is what this letter tells me. Listen:
  (They all draw nearer; she reads aloud):
  Mademoiselle,
  You must submit to the wishes
  Of the Cardinal, however hard that may be for you.
  That is why, to place
  These lines in your charming hands, I have chosen a most holy,
  Most intelligent and discreet Capuchin;
  We desire him to give you, in your own home,
  The nuptial
  (She turns the page):
  blessing at once.
  Christian must secretly become your husband;
  I am sending him to you. He displeases you. Resign yourself.
  Remember that Heaven will bless your zeal,
  And be entirely assured, Mademoiselle,
  Of the respect of him who was and who shall be
  Always your most humble and most... et cetera.

THE CAPUCHIN (beaming):
  Worthy lord!... I said so. I had no fears!
  It could only concern something holy!

ROXANE (softly to Christian):
  Do I not read letters very well?

CHRISTIAN:
  Hm!

ROXANE (aloud, despairingly):
  Ah!... It is dreadful!

THE CAPUCHIN (who has directed the light of his lantern onto Cyrano):
  Is it you?

CHRISTIAN:
  It is I!

THE CAPUCHIN (turning the light toward him and, as though a doubt
  occurred to him on seeing his beauty):
  But...

ROXANE (quickly):
  Postscript:
  Give the convent one hundred and twenty pistoles.

THE CAPUCHIN:
  Worthy,
  Worthy lord!
  (To Roxane):
  Do you resign yourself?

ROXANE (like a martyr):
  I resign myself!
  (While Ragueneau opens the door for the Capuchin, whom Christian invites
  to enter, she says softly to Cyrano):
  You—keep De Guiche here! He is going to come!
  Do not let him enter until...

CYRANO:
  Understood!
  (To the Capuchin):
  To bless them,
  you need?...

THE CAPUCHIN:
  A quarter of an hour.

CYRANO (pushing them all toward the house):
  Go! I shall remain!

ROXANE (to Christian):
  Come!...
  (They enter.)



Scene XII.

Cyrano, alone.


CYRANO:
  How can I make De Guiche lose a quarter of an hour?
  (He rushes to the bench and climbs the wall toward the balcony):
  There!... Let us climb!... I have my plan!...
  (The theorbos begin playing a mournful phrase):
  Oh! It is a man!
  (The tremolo becomes sinister):
  Oh! Oh!
  This time it is one!...
  (He is on the balcony; he pulls his felt hat down over his eyes, removes his
  sword, wraps himself in his cloak, then leans over and looks outside):
  No, it is not too high!...
  (He climbs over the balusters and, pulling toward himself the long branch of one of
  the trees that extend over the garden wall, grips it with both hands,
  ready to let himself drop):
  I am going to disturb this atmosphere slightly!...
